title: Consistent hashing ring
description: Consistent hashing maps both data keys and servers onto the same hash ring, so each key belongs to the first server clockwise from its hash. When a server joins or leaves, only the keys adjacent to it on the ring move — the rest of the data stays put. This is the foundation of nearly every sharded vector store and distributed cache.
mechanism: Hash the server identifiers and the keys with the same function (for example MD5 or xxHash), sort the points on a 0..2^128 ring, and walk clockwise from a key's hash to find its owner. Membership changes only remap the arcs touching the changed server.
algo: Ring lookup is a binary search over sorted server tokens: O(log S) per key for S servers. Key movement on membership change is O(K/S) keys on average.
complexity: O(log S) lookup; O(K/S) keys move per membership change

title: Virtual nodes (vnodes)
description: A plain hash ring gives each server one token, which leads to lopsided shards when servers differ in capacity or the hash function clusters. Virtual nodes give every physical server many tokens spread around the ring, so each server owns many small arcs instead of one big one. Load evens out, and removing a server spreads its keys across everyone instead of dumping them on one neighbor.
mechanism: Assign each physical server V virtual tokens (for example 128 or 256) at hash(server_id + '#' + str(i)). The owner of a key is the physical server behind the nearest virtual token clockwise. Heterogeneous hardware gets proportionally more vnodes.
algo: With V vnodes per server, the standard deviation of keys per server drops roughly by sqrt(V). Lookup stays O(log(S*V)).
demo:
import hashlib, collections

def h(x):
    return int(hashlib.md5(x.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)

def spread(nodes, vnodes, nkeys=20000):
    pts = sorted((h('%s#%d' % (n, i)), n) for n in nodes for i in range(vnodes))
    toks = [t for t, _ in pts]
    import bisect
    cnt = collections.Counter()
    for k in range(nkeys):
        kh = h('vec:%d' % k)
        j = bisect.bisect_left(toks, kh) % len(toks)
        cnt[pts[j][1]] += 1
    return cnt

for v in (1, 64):
    c = spread(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'], v)
    vals = sorted(c.values())
    print('vnodes=%d -> min %d max %d (ideal 5000)' % (v, vals[0], vals[-1]))

title: Shard key design
description: The shard key decides which shard owns each record, and a bad choice creates hot shards that throttle the whole cluster. Good shard keys have high cardinality, spread writes evenly, and keep the queries you actually run on one shard. For vector workloads the key is often a tenant id, a collection id, or a hash of the vector id — never a timestamp or a monotonically increasing id alone.
mechanism: Hash the chosen key fields (never the raw vector bytes) to pick a shard; keep a compound key of (tenant, vector_id) when multi-tenancy matters. Measure shard write rates and rebalance the key choice if one shard exceeds the mean by a wide margin.
algo: Key selection is O(1) per write. Hotness detection is a streaming heavy-hitters sketch (Count-Min) over shard ids: O(1) amortized per write.
complexity: O(1) per key; hotness sketch O(1) amortized
demo:
import hashlib, collections

def shard_of(key, n):
    return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % n

N = 8
bad = collections.Counter(shard_of('2024-01-%02d' % (i // 1000), N) for i in range(8000))
good = collections.Counter(shard_of('tenant-%d:vec-%d' % (i % 500, i), N) for i in range(8000))
print('monotonic-ish key :', sorted(bad.values()))
print('high-cardinality  :', sorted(good.values()))
print('ideal per shard   :', 8000 // N)

title: Range vs hash partitioning
description: Hash partitioning spreads keys pseudo-randomly and gives even load, but it destroys ordering — range scans must fan out to every shard. Range partitioning keeps nearby keys together so range queries hit one shard, but sequential writes pile onto the last range and create a hotspot. Vector stores usually hash-partition by id and keep range-friendly metadata (like timestamps) in a separate ordered index.
mechanism: Hash mode: shard = hash(key) mod N. Range mode: shard = the range bucket containing the sort key, looked up in a routing table. Hybrid systems hash the id for the vector payload and range-partition a metadata index for filtered queries.
algo: Hash routing is O(1). Range routing is a routing-table lookup, O(log R) for R ranges, plus periodic range-split decisions.
complexity: O(1) hash routing; O(log R) range routing
demo:
import hashlib, bisect

N = 4
def hash_shard(k):
    return int(hashlib.md5(str(k).encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % N

bounds = [250, 500, 750]
def range_shard(k):
    return bisect.bisect_right(bounds, k)

seq = list(range(1000))
h = [hash_shard(k) for k in seq]
r = [range_shard(k) for k in seq]
print('hash : first-100 keys land on shards', sorted(set(h[:100])))
print('range: first-100 keys land on shards', sorted(set(r[:100])))
print('range scan 100..200 touches shards:', sorted(set(r[100:201])))
print('hash  scan 100..200 touches shards:', sorted(set(h[100:201])))

title: Replication factor and quorums
description: Each shard is copied to R replicas so one dead machine does not lose data. Reads and writes use quorums: a write succeeds when W replicas acknowledge and a read succeeds when R replicas answer, with W + R > N guaranteeing the read sees the latest write. Vector stores tune W and R per workload — W=ALL for ingest correctness, R=1 for latency-sensitive approximate search.
mechanism: The coordinator sends the write to all N replicas and waits for W acknowledgements; reads query R replicas and reconcile versions by timestamp or vector clock. Hinted handoff and read-repair converge replicas that missed writes.
algo: Quorum latency is the W-th (or R-th) order statistic of replica latencies. Availability holds while at least W (write) or R (read) replicas are reachable.
complexity: O(W) write fan-out; O(R) read fan-out
demo:
import random

random.seed(7)
N, W, R = 3, 2, 2
replicas = [{'v': 0, 'ts': 0} for _ in range(N)]
clock = 0

def write(val):
    global clock
    clock += 1
    order = random.sample(range(N), N)
    acked = 0
    for i in order:  # fastest replicas ack first
        replicas[i] = {'v': val, 'ts': clock}
        acked += 1
        if acked == W:
            break
    return acked

def read():
    got = random.sample(replicas, R)
    return max(got, key=lambda x: x['ts'])['v']

write(10); write(20)
print('replica states:', replicas)
print('quorum read sees:', read(), '(W+R>N guarantees latest)')
# kill one replica's updates: writes still succeed with W=2 of 3
replicas[0] = {'v': 0, 'ts': 0}
write(30)
print('after killing a replica, read sees:', read())

title: Partition-aware request routing
description: A client that knows the shard map sends each request straight to the owning shard — one network hop, no coordinator bottleneck. The shard map is cached client-side and refreshed on version mismatch. Without partition awareness every request funnels through a coordinator, which becomes the latency and throughput ceiling of the cluster.
mechanism: The client fetches the shard map (key range or hash ring plus replica addresses) at startup, caches it with a version number, and routes locally. On a stale-map error the server returns the current map version and the client refreshes and retries once.
algo: Local routing is O(1) per request after the map is cached. Map refresh is O(S) to fetch S shard entries, amortized over thousands of requests.
complexity: O(1) per request; O(S) per map refresh

title: Hot shard detection and mitigation
description: Even with good hashing, a celebrity tenant or a viral embedding can hammer one shard while the rest idle. Hot shard mitigation watches per-shard request rates, flags outliers, and either splits the hot shard or replicates its hottest keys to cooler shards. Detection must be fast (seconds, not minutes) because a hot shard degrades tail latency for the whole service.
mechanism: Each shard reports request rate and p99 latency on a short window; the controller computes z-scores across shards and marks |z| > 3 as hot. Mitigation: split the shard's key range, add read replicas for the hot keys, or move the hot tenant's vnodes.
algo: Rate tracking is O(1) per request with a sliding-window counter. Z-score scan is O(S) per control loop over S shards.
complexity: O(1) per request; O(S) per control loop
demo:
import random, statistics

random.seed(3)
S = 8
rates = [random.gauss(1000, 60) for _ in range(S)]
rates[5] = 4200  # shard 5 goes hot

mean = statistics.mean(rates)
stdev = statistics.pstdev(rates)
hot = [i for i, r in enumerate(rates) if abs((r - mean) / stdev) > 2.5]
print('per-shard req/s:', [int(r) for r in rates])
print('mean=%.0f stdev=%.0f -> hot shards:' % (mean, stdev), hot)
# mitigation: split shard 5 into two, halving its load
rates[5] /= 2
rates.append(rates[5])
print('after split, max shard load: %.0f req/s' % max(rates))

title: Rebalancing on membership change
description: When servers are added or removed, data must move so every shard again holds its fair share — without dropping queries mid-move. The standard approach streams the affected key ranges to their new owners while both old and new owners can serve reads, then atomically flips the shard map. Backfill runs with a bandwidth cap so rebalancing never starves live traffic.
mechanism: Compute the new ring, diff it against the old to find moved ranges, and stream those ranges in the background with checksums. Reads are dual-served during the move; the map version flips only after the new owner acknowledges the full range.
algo: Data moved is O(K/S) per changed server. Streaming is bandwidth-capped at B bytes/s, so rebalance time is roughly moved_bytes / B.
complexity: O(K/S) keys moved; time ~ bytes / bandwidth_cap

title: Cross-shard scatter-gather queries
description: A nearest-neighbor query over a sharded vector index must ask every shard for its local top-k and then merge the candidates — scatter-gather. Each shard returns its k best with distances; the coordinator merges, re-sorts, and trims to the global top-k. The pattern is simple but the tail latency is the slowest shard's latency, so hedged requests and per-shard deadlines matter.
mechanism: Fan the query out to all S shards in parallel with a deadline; collect each shard's (id, distance) pairs; k-way merge by distance and take the first k. Optionally re-rank the merged shortlist with exact distances for higher recall.
algo: Per-shard cost is the local ANN query; merge is O(S*k log(S*k)). Network cost is one round trip per shard in parallel.
complexity: O(S*k log(S*k)) merge; latency = slowest shard
demo:
import random, math, heapq

random.seed(11)
# 4 shards, each holding 250 random 2-D vectors
shards = [[[random.gauss(0, 1), random.gauss(0, 1)] for _ in range(250)] for _ in range(4)]
query = [0.3, -0.2]
K = 5

def dist(a, b):
    return math.dist(a, b)

cands = []
for s in shards:  # scatter: each shard returns local top-K
    top = heapq.nsmallest(K, ((dist(v, query), v) for v in s))
    cands.extend(top)
global_top = heapq.nsmallest(K, cands)  # gather: merge + trim
print('global top-%d distances:' % K, [round(d, 3) for d, _ in global_top])
# exact brute force over everything, for comparison
allv = [v for s in shards for v in s]
exact = heapq.nsmallest(K, (dist(v, query) for v in allv))
print('exact  top-%d distances:' % K, [round(d, 3) for d in exact])

title: Shard splitting and merging
description: A shard that outgrows its machine is split into two children, each taking half the key range; two underused shards are merged back into one. Splits must be online: the parent keeps serving while children backfill, and the map flips atomically when both children report ready. Splitting is the main way a sharded vector index grows past its original shard count without downtime.
mechanism: Pick a split point (median key or median hash), create two child shards, stream each half with a snapshot plus the write-ahead log tail, then update the shard map version so routers see the children. Merging reverses the process once both shards sit below the low-water mark.
algo: Split cost is proportional to the shard's data size (one full copy streamed). Split-point selection is O(n) over sampled keys or O(1) at the hash midpoint.
demo:
import hashlib

def h(x):
    return int(hashlib.md5(x.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)

RING = 2 ** 128
keys = ['vec:%d' % i for i in range(4000)]
# one shard owns the whole ring; split at the midpoint
mid = RING // 2
left = [k for k in keys if h(k) < mid]
right = [k for k in keys if h(k) >= mid]
print('before split: 1 shard holds %d keys' % len(keys))
print('after split : left=%d right=%d (ideal 2000/2000)' % (len(left), len(right)))
print('split serves the same keys, no downtime: total =', len(left) + len(right))

title: IVF partition lists for vectors
description: Inverted-file (IVF) indexes partition the vector space itself: k-means learns a few thousand centroids, and every vector is assigned to its nearest centroid's list. A query visits only the nprobe nearest lists instead of the whole dataset. Sharding then maps whole IVF lists to machines, so each shard owns a coherent region of vector space and queries route to the shards holding the nearest lists.
mechanism: Train centroids on a sample, assign each vector to argmin distance over centroids, and store postings per list. At query time compute distances to all centroids (cheap), pick the nprobe closest lists, and search only those — on whichever shards own them.
algo: Assignment is O(C*d) per vector for C centroids of dimension d. Query cost is O(C*d + nprobe*(N/C)*d) versus O(N*d) brute force.
complexity: O(C*d + nprobe*N*d/C) per query vs O(N*d) brute force
demo:
import random, math

random.seed(5)
D, N, C, NPROBE = 8, 4000, 16, 3
vecs = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(N)]
centroids = random.sample(vecs, C)

def dist(a, b):
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)))

lists = [[] for _ in range(C)]
for v in vecs:  # assign to nearest centroid
    lists[min(range(C), key=lambda c: dist(v, centroids[c]))].append(v)

q = [random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)]
order = sorted(range(C), key=lambda c: dist(q, centroids[c]))[:NPROBE]
scanned = sum(len(lists[c]) for c in order)
cands = [v for c in order for v in lists[c]]
best = min(cands, key=lambda v: dist(v, q))
exact = min(vecs, key=lambda v: dist(v, q))
print('scanned %d of %d vectors (%.1f%%)' % (scanned, N, 100.0 * scanned / N))
print('IVF best distance %.4f vs exact %.4f' % (dist(best, q), dist(exact, q)))

title: Geo-sharding and locality
description: Geo-sharding pins data to the region closest to the users who query it, cutting round-trip latency from hundreds of milliseconds to tens. Writes go to the local region and replicate asynchronously elsewhere; reads stay local. The hard part is the routing policy — by user region, by data regulation (data residency laws), and by failover priority when a region goes dark.
mechanism: Shard map carries a region tag per shard; the router picks the nearest healthy region for the request's origin. Async replication ships the write-ahead log cross-region; conflicts resolve by last-write-wins or CRDT merge.
algo: Routing adds one region lookup O(1). Cross-region replication lag is the 99th percentile of the inter-region link, typically 50-200 ms.
complexity: O(1) routing; replication lag = p99 inter-region RTT

title: Failure detection and failover
description: A sharded cluster must notice a dead shard in seconds and promote a replica without human help. Gossip-based failure detectors (like SWIM) let every node independently suspect failures and converge on agreement; the coordinator then reassigns the shard's token ranges to healthy replicas. False positives are the enemy — an aggressive detector that flaps causes constant rebalancing storms.
mechanism: Nodes gossip heartbeats with incarnation numbers; a node that misses T heartbeats is marked suspect, and after a further timeout it is marked dead. The shard map version bumps, routers refresh, and a replica takes over the token range while a replacement backfills.
algo: Gossip converges in O(log N) rounds. Detection latency is roughly T_heartbeat * missed_threshold, tunable against false-positive rate.
complexity: O(log N) gossip rounds; detection ~ heartbeats x threshold

title: Metadata service and shard map
description: The shard map — which key range lives on which server — is the cluster's source of truth, and it needs its own strongly consistent home. A metadata service (often Raft-backed) stores versioned shard maps; every router caches the map and every data node heartbeats its ranges. Split-brain maps are worse than downtime, so map updates go through consensus, never through gossip.
mechanism: Shard map versions are proposed to the Raft group; on commit, data nodes pull the new version and routers learn it lazily via version-mismatch errors. Each map entry is (range_start, range_end, primary, replicas[], version).
algo: Map lookup is O(log R) over R ranges (or O(1) with a hash ring). Consensus commit is O(N) messages for N metadata nodes, off the data path.
complexity: O(log R) lookup; consensus off the data path
demo:
import bisect

class ShardMap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.version = 0
        self.ranges = []  # (start, end, primary)
    def commit(self, ranges):  # consensus commit: all-or-nothing
        self.version += 1
        self.ranges = sorted(ranges)
    def locate(self, key_hash):
        starts = [r[0] for r in self.ranges]
        i = bisect.bisect_right(starts, key_hash) - 1
        s, e, primary = self.ranges[i]
        assert s <= key_hash < e, 'key outside map!'
        return primary, self.version

m = ShardMap()
R = 2 ** 32
m.commit([(0, R // 2, 'shard-a'), (R // 2, R, 'shard-b')])
for kh in (10, R // 2 - 1, R // 2, R - 1):
    print('hash %d -> %s (map v%d)' % (kh, m.locate(kh)[0], m.locate(kh)[1]))

title: Benchmarking a sharded vector index
description: A benchmark proves the shard design actually holds up: it measures queries per second, p50/p99 latency, and recall@k as shard count and nprobe vary. The honest setup uses a public ANN benchmark dataset, warms up the caches, and reports the full latency distribution — not just the mean. Scaling efficiency (QPS per shard) tells you whether adding machines is worth the money.
mechanism: Load a ground-truth dataset (queries plus exact nearest neighbors), run the sharded system at increasing concurrency, and record per-query latency and recall = |found intersect truth| / k. Plot QPS and p99 against shard count to find the knee where coordination overhead wins.
algo: Recall@k = |retrieved_k intersect true_k| / k. Scaling efficiency = QPS(S) / (S * QPS(1)). Benchmark time is O(Q * query_cost) for Q queries.
demo:
import random, math, time

random.seed(21)
D, N, Q, K = 16, 2000, 50, 5
vecs = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(D)] for _ in range(N)]
queries = random.sample(vecs, Q)

def dist(a, b):
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)))

def brute(q):
    return sorted(range(N), key=lambda i: dist(vecs[i], q))[:K]

def approx(q, sample=400):  # toy ANN: search a random 20% sample
    idx = random.sample(range(N), sample)
    return sorted(idx, key=lambda i: dist(vecs[i], q))[:K]

lat, rec = [], []
for q in queries:
    truth = set(brute(q))
    t = time.perf_counter()
    got = approx(q)
    lat.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)
    rec.append(len(set(got) & truth) / K)
lat.sort()
print('queries=%d  mean recall@%d=%.3f' % (Q, K, sum(rec) / Q))
print('p50 latency=%.2f ms  p99 latency=%.2f ms' % (lat[len(lat)//2], lat[int(len(lat)*0.99)]))
